qs.q: Which anatomical structure is attached to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus?
qs.e: The deltoid muscle inserts into the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. The lesser tubercle receives the subscapularis tendon instead.
qs.s: Limb Anatomy Revision — Lower & Upper Limb: MCQs

qs.q: A 20-year-old woman has 6 months of symmetrical proximal muscle weakness. Deltoid biopsy shows inflammatory infiltrates and focal myofiber necrosis. ANA and anti-Mi-2 are positive; Jo-1 is negative. Most likely additional finding?
qs.e: Anti-Mi-2 positive + proximal muscle weakness + inflammatory myopathy = dermatomyositis. The violaceous heliotrope skin rash is a characteristic feature, often subtle and limited to the face.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The deltoid is a triangular muscle covering the shoulder, key for arm abduction beyond 70°. Its function depends on intact axillary nerve and thoracoacromial blood supply.

sections.p: The deltoid is the primary mover for arm abduction beyond 70°, acting as a powerful shoulder stabilizer and a key landmark for shoulder surgeries.
b: Triangular shape; three distinct fibers: anterior, middle, posterior

sections.p: Originates from the lateral third of clavicle, acromion, and spine of scapula. Inserts on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.
b: Anterior fibers: flexion and medial rotation; middle: abduction; posterior: extension and lateral rotation

sections.p: Superficial to the axillary nerve and posterior cord of brachial plexus. Lies over the subacromial space and beneath the acromion.
b: Deltoid is the most superficial muscle over the shoulder joint

sections.p: Primarily from the thoracoacromial artery (clavicular, acromial, deltoid branches) and the posterior humeral circumflex artery.
b: Adequate perfusion essential for healing after injury or surgery

t.b: Shows patency of thoracoacromial branches; abnormal flow suggests vascular injury or compression

sections.p: Axillary nerve (C5‑C6) innervates all fibers; injury leads to loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
b: Weakness in abduction beyond 70° is a red flag for axillary nerve damage

t.b: Detects denervation potentials in deltoid; confirms axillary nerve injury

sections.p: Primary action is abduction beyond 70°. Secondary actions include flexion, extension, medial and lateral rotation depending on fiber group.
b: Deltoid works with supraspinatus for initial abduction up to 30°

sections.p: Common injuries include rotator cuff tears, deltoid contusions, and axillary nerve palsy. In low-resource settings, infections like tetanus or septic arthritis can damage the muscle.
b: Regimental badge sensory loss indicates axillary nerve injury

t.b: Identifies tendon tears or muscle edema; useful when CT is unavailable

sections.p: Ask patients to abduct arm to 90°; inability indicates axillary nerve or deltoid pathology. Palpate the acromion and clavicle to locate the muscle belly.
b: Deltoid is the most superficial muscle over the shoulder; easy to palpate

whenToSeekHelp: Severe shoulder pain with inability to abduct, sudden loss of sensation over the regimental badge, or swelling suggesting compartment syndrome

faq.a: Axillary nerve injury, trauma, or compressive lesions like tumors.

faq.q: How is a deltoid tear diagnosed?
faq.a: MRI shows tendon discontinuity; ultrasound can be used if MRI is unavailable.

faq.q: Can the deltoid recover after axillary nerve damage?
faq.a: Recovery depends on nerve regeneration; early physiotherapy improves outcomes.
